summary: Hopewell Tower: an 80-ft steel tower built in 1935 with federal funds and CCC/French Creek labor; registered 2012; current access not verified.

facts.design: 80-foot steel McClintic-Marshall tower with 7x7 foot cab
facts.status_note: The 2012 register entry includes photos of the cab interior, which suggests it was standing then. No later status report was found.

events.note: Department of Forests and Waters selected a site in Union Township; about ten acres deeded for $1 by Mrs. Louise Brooks of Birdsboro
80-foot steel tower erected with federal funds; NHLR credits the CCC/French Creek Recreation project
Tower placed in service May 1, 1935; a picnic park was planned around it
Works Progress Administration began finishing the access road to the tower, which a 1936 item calls the Williams Hill fire tower
George H. Wolf named as lookout in a Reading Times item
About 50 men cleared brush and built a 1 1/2 mile road at the Hopewell fire tower
Forest Fire Lookout Association formed at a meeting in the District 17 garage at French Creek State Park, followed by a tour of the Hopewell tower and ground cabin (early 1990)
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register on May 13, 2012

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1935 report and the NHLR both give 80 feet. A 1939 item gives 90 feet for a tower in the Geigertown area, which may be this tower or another. The story uses 80 feet.
A 1933 item names Mrs. Louise Brooks of Birdsboro as the donor. A 1934 item names Mrs. Edward Brooke of Birdsboro. The story names the 1933 donor and notes the variant.

The NHLR places the tower in William Penn Forest. The 1930s items place it in Union Township near Hopewell Furnace, and the FFLA history places its 1990 meeting at the French Creek State Park garage. I could not reconcile the public-land names from these pages.
A 1933 plan gave the site a 960-foot elevation. The NHLR gives 998 feet (304 m). The planned site and the built site may differ, or the figures may be measured differently.
The 1935 item names the Department of Forests and Waters, the agency of that time. The NHLR now names the Pennsylvania Bureau of Forestry.

notes_for_editor: Build history rests on a 1933 to 1939 run of newspaper items, the NHLR entry, and the FFLA history. The Weebly page has nothing after 1939, so staffing and fate after that are unverified. A trail-app listing reportedly says the public cannot climb the tower; that page returned HTTP 403 and is not cited. The NHLR photos (cab interior, cabin) have no image URLs captured, so none are listed. The brief's record matches the NHLR (1935 built, 2012 registered, 24.4 m).
